title: Rules, Rights & Citizenship
description: Rules, rights and citizenship: why rules matter, fairness and voting, children's rights, the Constitution of India, democracy and elections, the three branches of government, the courts and rule of law, and active citizenship. Non-partisan and grounded in constitutional values.

lessons.title: Rules Help Us
objectives: Name rules at home and school
Explain how rules keep us safe and fair
explanation: Rules tell us what to do and what not to do. At home, a rule might be "wash hands before eating". At school, "raise your hand to speak".
Rules keep us safe: "walk, don't run, near the pool". Rules keep things fair: "take turns on the slide".
When everyone follows rules, it's easier to live and play together happily.

vocabulary.meaning: an instruction about what to do or not do

examples: "Hold hands when crossing the road" — a safety rule.
"Share the crayons" — a fairness rule.

story.title: The Playground Without Rules
story.text: One day, the animals decided to have no rules at the playground. Everyone pushed to the slide, the swings got tangled, and little Rangi got knocked over. "Maybe rules aren't so bad," said Kiko. They made three rules: take turns, be gentle, help anyone who falls. The playground was fun again.

lessons.title: Let's Vote!
objectives: Take part in a simple vote
Accept a group decision even if it wasn't their choice
explanation: When a group must choose, everyone can vote. Each person chooses once — by raising a hand or putting a token in a box. The choice with the most votes wins.
Voting is fair because everyone gets one vote, and everyone's vote counts the same.
If your choice doesn't win, it's okay to feel disappointed — but we accept the result and maybe try again next time.

lessons.title: My Rights
objectives: Name rights that all children have
Explain why rights matter
explanation: Rights are things every person should have just because they are human. Children have special rights too, agreed by almost every country in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), which India signed.
Children have the right to a name, to go to school, to healthcare, to play, to be safe from harm, and to have their opinions heard on things that affect them.
Rights belong to every child, everywhere — whatever their gender, religion, language, family or ability.

context.text: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989; India ratified it in 1992. India's Right to Education Act (2009) makes education a right for children aged 6–14.

examples: Going to school is a right.
Being kept safe from harm is a right.

story.title: The Rights Kite
story.text: Zuri made a kite with a ribbon for each right: school, health, play, safety, being heard. When the wind blew, all the ribbons flew together. "Every child should have a kite like this," she said. "And no one should cut the ribbons."

lessons.title: Two Sides of a Coin
objectives: Match rights with responsibilities
Explain respecting others' rights
explanation: Rights and responsibilities go together, like two sides of a coin. If I have the right to learn, I have a responsibility to try my best and not stop others learning.
If I have the right to be safe, I have a responsibility not to hurt others. If I have the right to be heard, I should listen to others too.
Respecting other people's rights is how we protect everyone's rights.
examples: Right to play → responsibility to share the playground.
Right to a clean environment → responsibility not to litter.

story.title: The Noisy Classroom
story.text: During reading time, Kiko kept talking loudly. Momo couldn't read. "I have the right to talk!" said Kiko. "And I have the right to learn," said Momo. The teacher explained, "Your right to talk comes with a responsibility not to stop others learning. Let's talk at break time." Kiko agreed.

lessons.title: Our National Flag
objectives: Describe the national flag and its colours
Name national symbols and national days
explanation: India's national flag is the tricolour: saffron at the top, white in the middle with a navy blue Ashoka Chakra (a wheel with 24 spokes), and green at the bottom.

Other national symbols include the national emblem (the Lion Capital of Ashoka from Sarnath), the national anthem "Jana Gana Mana" by Rabindranath Tagore, and the national song "Vande Mataram" by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay.
Independence Day (15 August) marks freedom from British rule in 1947. Republic Day (26 January) marks the Constitution coming into effect in 1950.

context.text: The flag was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947; the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
The flag's colours are commonly explained as courage and sacrifice (saffron), truth and peace (white), and faith, fertility and prosperity (green); explanations vary.

examples: Flag hoisting on Independence Day at school.

story.title: The Flag at School
story.text: On Independence Day morning, Ivaan's school gathered in the courtyard. As the principal hoisted the tricolour, flower petals fluttered down from its folds. Everyone stood straight and sang "Jana Gana Mana". Ivaan counted the spokes of the chakra in a picture later: twenty-four!

lessons.title: India's Rulebook
objectives: Explain what a constitution is
Name some fundamental rights and duties
explanation: A constitution is the highest set of rules for a country. It says how the government works and what rights citizens have. India's Constitution, one of the longest in the world, was written by the Constituent Assembly between 1946 and 1949.
Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the drafting committee. The Preamble begins "We, the people of India" and promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

Fundamental Rights include equality before law, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, protection from exploitation, and the right to constitutional remedies. Fundamental Duties include respecting the Constitution and flag, protecting the environment and developing a scientific temper.

context.text: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (now observed as Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950.

vocabulary.meaning: the highest set of rules of a country
basic rights protected by the Constitution

examples: Freedom of speech lets people express opinions.
Protecting the environment is a fundamental duty.

story.title: We, the People
story.text: In 1949, after nearly three years of debate, members of the Constituent Assembly — from many regions, religions and backgrounds, including 15 women — signed the Constitution. Their first words were "We, the people of India". The rulebook belonged not to kings or rulers, but to the people.

lessons.title: Government by the People
objectives: Define democracy and representative democracy
Explain universal adult franchise and minority rights
explanation: Democracy means government by the people. In a direct democracy, people vote on every decision. In a representative democracy, like India, people elect representatives to make laws for them.
India has universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18 or older can vote, regardless of religion, caste, gender, wealth or education — one person, one vote.
In a healthy democracy, the majority decides, but the rights of minorities are protected, and people can criticise the government freely and peacefully.

context.text: The voting age in India was lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988). India's first general elections were held in 1951–52.

vocabulary.meaning: a person elected to act for others
a smaller group within a larger population

examples: Electing a Member of Parliament (MP) for your constituency.
Protecting freedom of religion for all groups.

story.title: The World's Biggest Election
story.text: In India's first general election in 1951–52, millions of people voted for the first time, many of whom could not read. Party symbols — like a pair of bullocks or a lamp — helped them choose. Today, India's elections are the largest in the world, with polling booths even in remote mountains and forests.

lessons.title: Election Day
objectives: Describe the steps of an election
Explain safeguards for free and fair elections
explanation: The Election Commission of India, an independent constitutional body, organises elections. The country is divided into constituencies; each elects one representative.

Before voting, candidates campaign under a Model Code of Conduct. On election day, voters show ID, get indelible ink on a finger, and vote secretly using an Electronic Voting Machine (EVM). A VVPAT slip lets voters verify their vote.
Votes are counted, and the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins. The party or coalition with a majority in the Lok Sabha forms the government.

vocabulary.meaning: an area that elects a representative

examples: Indelible ink on a voter's left index finger.

story.title: Grandmother Votes
story.text: Ivaan went with his grandmother to the polling station at his school. She showed her voter ID, got a purple ink mark on her finger and stepped behind a screen. Beep! She came out smiling. "Nobody knows who I voted for," she whispered, "and that's exactly how it should be."

lessons.title: Who Does What?
objectives: Describe the roles of the three branches
Explain checks and balances and federalism
explanation: The legislature makes laws. India's Parliament has the Lok Sabha (elected directly by the people) and the Rajya Sabha (elected mainly by state legislatures), plus the President.

The executive carries out laws. The President is head of state; the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers run the government. The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes; the Supreme Court is the highest court.

Checks and balances stop any branch from becoming too powerful: courts can strike down unconstitutional laws; Parliament can question ministers. India is federal: power is shared between the Union and the states.

vocabulary.meaning: the branch that carries out laws

examples: Parliament passing a budget.

story.title: The Three Friends' Agreement
story.text: Professor Hoot explained with a story: three friends ran a village. One wrote the rules, one carried them out, and one judged disputes. When the rule-carrier tried to ignore a rule, the judge stopped him. When the rule-writer wrote an unfair rule, the judge struck it down. "Each keeps the others honest," said Hoot.

lessons.title: No One Is Above the Law
objectives: Explain the rule of law
Describe how laws are made and how courts protect rights
explanation: The rule of law means everyone — ordinary citizens, officials and leaders — must obey the law, and laws apply equally to all.
A bill becomes a law after being debated and passed by both houses of Parliament and receiving the President's assent.

Courts protect rights: anyone accused of a crime has the right to a fair trial and a lawyer, and is presumed innocent until proven guilty. Through public interest litigation (PIL), citizens can approach courts on behalf of people whose rights are violated.

context.text: Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equality before the law; PILs became prominent in India from the late 1970s and 1980s.

vocabulary.meaning: everyone must obey laws that apply equally
a court case filed for the public good

examples: A senior official prosecuted for corruption.
A PIL leading to cleaner air measures in cities.

story.title: The Case for Clean Air
story.text: Citizens worried about air pollution in a city filed a public interest litigation. The court examined evidence from scientists and ordered actions to reduce pollution. "The court can't solve everything," one lawyer said, "but it reminded everyone that the right to life includes the right to breathe."

lessons.title: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
objectives: Explain key political concepts
Compare ideas of major thinkers fairly
explanation: Political philosophy asks: What makes government legitimate? How should liberty and equality be balanced? Thinkers from many traditions, from Kautilya's Arthashastra to Locke, Rousseau and Mill, offered different answers.

Mahatma Gandhi developed satyagraha — nonviolent resistance based on truth — and swaraj, self-rule both political and personal. Dr Ambedkar warned that political democracy needs social democracy: liberty, equality and fraternity in everyday life, not just in law.

Political ideologies (on a spectrum from more state action to more market freedom, more tradition to more change) offer different priorities. Good citizens understand views they disagree with and argue respectfully with evidence.

context.text: Political ideas are contested; this lesson presents thinkers' views for understanding and does not endorse any party or ideology.
Ambedkar's warning about social democracy comes from his speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949.

vocabulary.meaning: equality and fraternity in social life

examples: The Salt March (1930) as satyagraha.
Debates over the role of government in healthcare.

story.title: A Warning and a Hope
story.text: On 25 November 1949, the day before the Constitution was adopted, Dr Ambedkar told the Assembly that India was entering a life of contradictions: equality in politics but inequality in social and economic life. He urged the nation to remove these contradictions — a challenge students still debate today.

lessons.title: Being an Active Citizen
objectives: Describe peaceful ways to participate in civic life
Explain global institutions and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
prerequisites: Understands rule of law and rights
explanation: Citizenship isn't only voting. Citizens can file Right to Information (RTI) requests to see government records, write petitions, attend public meetings, volunteer, and engage peacefully in debate. Checking facts before sharing news is part of responsible citizenship.

Globally, the United Nations (founded 1945) works for peace, development and human rights. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) set out rights for all people; Hansa Mehta of India helped change its wording from "all men" to "all human beings are born free and equal".
Global challenges — climate change, pandemics, migration — require cooperation across borders. Global citizens think about how their actions affect people everywhere.

context.text: The Right to Information Act was passed in 2005. Hansa Mehta served on the UN Commission on Human Rights and is credited with the change to Article 1 of the UDHR.

vocabulary.meaning: Right to Information, a law letting citizens request government information
a formal request signed by people
someone who considers their role in the wider world

examples: An RTI request revealing how funds for a local road were spent.
Students joining an international climate project.

story.title: Hansa Mehta's Words
story.text: When the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was being drafted, the first article said "All men are born free and equal." Hansa Mehta, a delegate from India, argued that this could exclude women. The wording was changed to "All human beings." Her small change carried a huge meaning for half the world.
